extracted.intended_audience: legislators, constitutional designers, political theorists, and informed citizens (e.g., delegates to Congress)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and historical criteria for structuring republican government: separation and balance of powers, institutional safeguards (judiciary, censorship, magistracies), property and social policy limits, and dangers from faction, military expansion, and popular corruption. Draws on Roman examples to illustrate design lessons and pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three branches of power as a foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: That three branches of power have an unalterable foundation in nature; that they exist in every society natural and artificial; and that if all of them are not acknowledged in any constitution of government, it will be found to be imperfect, unstable, and soon enslaved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists a well-framed constitution must recognise three distinct branches (implicitly legislative, executive, judicial). Examples and historical authorities are cited to show universality. Failure to acknowledge them renders a constitution defective and liable to corruption or subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of legislative and executive authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative and executive authorities are naturally distinct; and that liberty and the laws depend entirely on a separation of them in the frame of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation is presented as essential to preserve liberty and the rule of law. The statement is applied directly to American states ('applicable to every State in America, in its individual capacity') and poses the question whether the same applies at the federal level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive must be empowered to defend itself (negative/veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative power is naturally and necessarily sovereign and supreme over the executive; and therefore that the latter must be made an essential branch of the former, even with a negative, or it will not be able to defend itself, but will be soon invaded, undermined, attacked, or in some way or other totally ruined and annihilated by the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that because legislatures are naturally superior, the executive requires institutional means (explicitly a 'negative'—i.e., a veto) to check legislative dominance and preserve the balance between branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of the three powers is wise but requires independence and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixture of the three powers in a commonwealth exhibits the fairest prospect of our species; on the other hand, the evils arising from the want of complete independence in each branch, and from an ineffectual balance, are clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises mixed government (e.g., Roman, English) but warns that unless each branch retains independence and the balance is effective, the mixture produces domestic contests and revolutions. Design should aim for both mixture and robust checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of law and regular judicial procedures protect rights and liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: By establishing a body of laws, and regular formal proceedings in the courts of justice, they have secured their own rights and liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure, codified laws and regular judicial procedure are credited with protecting citizens' rights; institutionalising legal processes reduces arbitrary power (Roman example used).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious toleration as a civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: In private every family were free to worship the gods in their own way; and in public, though certain forms were required, yet there was not any penalty annexed to the omission of them, the punishment of offences in this matter being left to the offended god. This is probably the source of that wise and humane toleration which does so much honour to the Romans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State design should avoid penal sanctions for private religious practice and limit state enforcement to public forms without criminal penalties; this fosters humane toleration and social stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multiple competing sources of legislation (fragmented legislative authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hence three distinct sources of laws—decrees of the senate, acts of the centuries, and resolutions of the tribes—were a source of division, disunion, and tumult, which never ceased to issue streams until the authority of the senate was destroyed and a dominatio plebis began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fragmentation of legislative authority into separate, competing legislative sources breeds division and instability. A clearer, more unified legislative structure or mechanisms to reconcile competing authorities is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate sacerdotal (religious) and military/civil functions to broaden eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The military and sacerdotal functions had before been united; they were now separated, and as the people thought, without profanation. The title of Consul was changed for that of Military Tribune; no sacerdotal function being included in the duties of this office, plebeians, though not qualified to be consuls, were elected military tribunes with consular power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional separation of religious and civil/military offices can remove formal barriers to participation by previously excluded classes, enabling broader access to high office while respecting religious scruples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of property and caution toward radical redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The project (of Tiberius Gracchus) seemed to be as ruinous to government as it was to the security of property, and tended to place members of the commonwealth by one rash and precipitate step in situations in which they were not at all qualified to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions that aggressive or abrupt land redistribution and similar measures undermine property security and governmental stability; reforms must consider practical governance and social qualifications, not only equity rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit-based selection and censorial oversight preserve institutions' dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The integrity and strict exercise of the censorial power guarded the authority of the senate, the dignity of the equestrian order, and the manners of the people in general; the wisest and most respected of the citizens, from every condition, were raised into office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms (like the censor) that evaluate and promote virtue, education, and merit for office help maintain institutional integrity and social order. Design should include offices/processes that screen and promote public virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware corruption from foreign conquest and imperial wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of the Roman arms abroad became the source of a ruinous corruption at home; the governing and the governed left separate interests, and were at variance from motives of avarice as well as ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expansion and the influx of wealth can create divergent interests between rulers and citizens and foster corruption; constitutional design needs safeguards (accountability, limits on spoils, oversight) to mitigate these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage popular assemblies and curb demagoguery to prevent mob rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A turbulent populace tyrannised in their turn over the conquerors of so many nations...they were corrupted by idleness and indigence; censors had taken the precaution to confine all citizens of mean or slavish extraction to four of the tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive enfranchisement or unchecked popular appeals (cheap corn, public shows, demagogues) can destabilise government. Institutional devices (tribal allocations, filters, representation structures) can moderate raw popular power while avoiding outright disenfranchisement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent concentration of extraordinary powers in temporary commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The decemvirs, intended only as a committee to prepare a draught for consideration, had so much credit with the people as to be vested with a temporary sovereignty, superseded the authority of the senate as well as the consuls, and had unlimited power over the lives and fortunes of their fellow-citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary or emergency bodies must be constrained by clear limits, term restrictions, and accountability; otherwise emergent commissions can usurp permanent power and destroy constitutional balances (example: decemvirs).
